tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

1	# Issue #141: Run practice: the last candidate of a budget-bound run goes unreviewed
2	
3	Opened by dat9uy at 2026-11-12T02:21:06Z. Text as of 2026-11-12T03:45:00Z.
4	
5	## Event
6	
7	On 2026-11-12, run 1 of `investigations/goal-prompt` (G-ZBM2RE, PR #140) stopped with its last candidate, H-YXSJEM at `5c5902d`, never reviewed. The two earlier candidates were reviewed, and each review found real defects (10 findings on `10566d4`, 8 on `b4f23b2`). The stop checkpoint says "all review limits closed" and does not name the missing review.
8	
9	The chain, from the run's transcript and the two trees:
10	
11	1. A review finding that is a case of a line becomes a limit, and `--limit` exists only on `hyp record`. So the runner recorded each review as its own Experiment: E-C3GGGJ reviewed `10566d4` and E-7QQ2DP reviewed `b4f23b2`.
12	2. Each candidate therefore cost two Experiments, a gate and a review. The run spent E-HQWTA0, E-C3GGGJ, E-Z5BTZR, E-7QQ2DP and E-NZR3GV (the gate of `5c5902d`), and the stop clause "5 Experiments have been recorded" ended it.
13	3. The default of 5 was set from G-D1CH1R's runs, where every Experiment gates a commit and review findings went straight into fix commits (one Experiment per candidate; run 5 used 4).
14	4. At 17:21:37 the runner wrote "E5 is the last Experiment the budget allows, so this fix commit must close everything." `skills/hyp-goal-run/SKILL.md` asks for "one review of each candidate commit's diff" before the stop. The prompt's stop clause and the skill conflict, and neither says which yields or that the gap is named at the stop.
15	
16	## Scope
17	
18	Core: the run practice of a Goal whose candidate is a commit (review, budget and stop report) in `hyp-goal-run`, and the stop clause `hyp prompt` prints. No self-review recipe is involved.
19	
20	## Rivals
21	
22	A tree holds this question; each option below is a rival Hypothesis, not a decision. The scenario that separates them: replay the G-ZBM2RE cut after R-8JQPWG (one Experiment left, a fix commit pending) and see whether the run stops with every candidate reviewed or with the gap named.
23	
24	- **H-one-experiment:** a candidate's review is part of its gate Experiment. One Result carries the test verdicts and the review's limits, so a candidate costs one Experiment again.
25	- **H-name-at-stop:** keep the practice; the stop checkpoint names each candidate without a review, so the gap is visible to the owner.
26	- **H-reserve-last:** when one Experiment remains, the runner reviews the current candidate instead of committing another fix, and stops with recorded limits.
27	- **H-raise-budget:** the default of `--experiments` rises (for example to 7) to fit a gate and a review per candidate.
28	
29	These can combine (H-name-at-stop with any other); the tree should say which hold alone.
30	
31	## Done means
32	
33	- A tree under this issue selects a rival, or a combination, from a run on the scenario above.
34	- After the change, a run that reaches its budget either has a review Result for its final candidate or names that candidate as unreviewed in the stop checkpoint.
35	
36	Part of #113. Observation log: run 1, entry R10.
37	
38	---
39	
40	Comment by the owner at 2026-11-12T03:04:10Z:
41	
42	Second event, 2026-11-12: run 2 of `investigations/goal-prompt` (actor `claude-g113-2`, session `d3fe6332`) ended the same way, with its last candidate unreviewed.
43	
44	It started with a fresh budget of 5 (`hyp prompt`'s clause "5 Results recorded under the actor") and spent it as:
45	
46	1. R-0E8PFH applies the owner's six answers.
47	2. R-KYKWH9 reviews `5c5902d`, closing run 1's gap; 1 limit.
48	3. R-28A8NB gates the fix commit `2284172`.
49	4. R-3YJ7T2 reviews `2284172`; 2 limits, and the run's own probes of both cases pass.
50	5. R-356DV0 gates `3cfd08d`, a commit that adds tests and spec text for those two passing cases.
51	
52	`3cfd08d` (H-FQ103R) is unreviewed. Unlike run 1, the stop names the gap: "3cfd08d needs a fresh review of its diff, and the cap left no room to run one."
53	
54	What this adds to the rivals:
55	
56	- **Against H-raise-budget.** A fresh budget did not help. Each review so far has led to a new commit (findings 10, 8, 1, 2), and each commit owes its own review, so any fixed budget ends on an unreviewed commit unless a review leads to no commit.
57	- **For H-reserve-last.** The last commit was not needed: both limits' probes passed on `2284172`, so a Result closing them on H-YTD2JG followed by the select would have ended on a reviewed candidate. A related rule to test with it: a case whose check already passes closes as a limit, not with a new commit.

1	---
2	name: hyp-goal-run
3	description: "Run a hyp tree under an owner's Goal and met rule as an unattended /goal, for a discovery Goal or a build Goal: act only on what OWED says the runner owes, test before asking, write readings the owner can answer, reassess the targets under the owner's answers, and stop with a report the owner can read from hyp status. Use when a /goal prompt names this skill, such as the one hyp prompt prints."
4	---
5	
6	The `/goal` prompt names the tree, your actor, the Goal, the stop and the Goal body's constraints; `hyp prompt <goal-id> --actor <actor>` prints it from the log. This skill says how to work until that stop. Use it with the hyp-prototype skill, which says how to add Questions, Hypotheses, Experiments and Results, and the hyp-verification skill, which says how to run an Experiment.
7	
8	## Start
9	
10	- Read the Goal first with `hyp show <goal-id>`, including its checkpoints, because `hyp status` does not print its met rule.
11	- Everything you need is in the tree. Do not read session logs, reports or memory about earlier runs.
12	- The Goal's body states the run's constraints under three headings: `May change:` (what you may write, and how), `Read only:` (what you may read but never change) and `Never:` (acts you never take). Obey them. A `/goal` prompt may narrow them, never widen them. If a step needs something they forbid, refer it with a reason or record a reading, and stop.
13	- A store may hold many Goals. Then `hyp status` prints only a GOALS table and one Awaiting owner list, so run `hyp status <goal-id>` wherever this skill says `hyp status`: OWED, LINES, the stop line and the last checkpoint are per Goal. Name the Goal with `--goal <goal-id>` on `hyp checkpoint`.
14	- Print `hyp status` at the end of every turn.
15	
16	## Work
17	
18	Act on what OWED in `hyp status` says the runner owes, and on nothing else. Plan only the next Experiment.
19	
20	- Use the Goal's must-fail cases as known-answer flaw cases, in the owner's terms.
21	- The recipe's checks may exist before the verdict rule, because `hyp add exp` pins them. Write and run no candidate until the rule is recorded on the Experiment.
22	- Try a new or changed check only on its cases' stand-ins, never on a candidate, until the rule is recorded. If a candidate shows a check is wrong anyway, do not just fix the check: write the case that shows it, in the Goal's terms with the outcome it must give, in a new version, and name that case in the Experiment body. A sentence that discloses a trial run pins nothing.
23	- `hyp record` and `hyp check` warn when a Result's text disagrees with its cited files: a verdict that a cited `verdict:` line contradicts, or a commit or hash in the observation or a limit that no cited file holds. Fix each one with a new Result that cites the file; a Result cannot change after it is recorded.
24	
25	## Build Goals
26	
27	A build Goal's candidate is a commit. Its practice:
28	
29	- Each commit you test is one Hypothesis under the Goal's question, with the branch and the commit in its title. Tie its subject before the run with `hyp subject <H> --base <commit>`. A fix is a new commit and a new Hypothesis that supersedes the old one (`hyp supersede <new> --old <old>`).
30	- Write the tree with the installed hyp. Compile the candidate to a separate path, and never replace an installed binary.
31	- Pin the gate as a recipe when the repository keeps one, so a script decides the verdict. When none does, the Experiment on a commit uses `--recipe none --rubric reading`: its body states the gate as the rule, and the Result cites the gate's logs.
32	- Before you run anything, write each Experiment's verdict rule in its body: the Goal's lines it aims at, red on the base and green on the candidate for each new test, a removal check for each refusal (remove the refusal and show which test fails), and `go vet ./...` and `go test ./... -count=1`, or the repository's own gate. For skill text, run the original and the candidate skills on the same eval cases.
33	- Keep the logs under `.tree/evidence/<E-id>/` and cite them in the Result.
34	- Before the stop, ask a fresh subagent for one review of each candidate commit's diff against the design and the Goal's lines. Give it the code, the lines and the keys already settled, with the owner's words; do not give it your conclusion. Ask it to label each finding with the line it is a case of, or none.
35	- Sort each finding: a case of a line is a `--limit` you close or, only if void, refer; a question about a line's meaning is a reading; a defect in text you may edit is a fix commit; anything else is an out-of-Goal finding, named in the stop checkpoint, and it never holds the select.
36	- The run may push its branch and open or update one PR. It never merges.
37	
38	## Before a trade-off
39	
40	Before a Question goes to the owner as a trade-off, add one structure that is not among the candidates, and the cheapest variant of each contradicted rival that would hold. Run them through a new version of the pinned recipe and record the Result. If a new structure holds every check, say in a checkpoint that the rule does not decide this Question.
41	
42	## Readings
43	
44	- When a verdict rests on your reading of a Goal line, write the other reading as a strict check: a separate named command in the recipe, with its own known answers, that sets no verdict. Say so in the Experiment's verdict rule, and run it on the same candidates. Record the reading with `hyp record --reading`, naming the check and which candidates fail it. If the recipe cannot test the other reading, say that in the reading.
45	- When a verdict rests on the word of a reading that is still open under AWAITING OWNER, or on an owner answer another Result already reads, record the same reading on that Result too, word for word, with the same `--reading-of` key if it has one: a reading holds only its own Result's Question, and hyp prints identical readings as one question and warns when the owner answers only one. Record a copy only on a Result that judged a Hypothesis whose verdict differs from the strict check's outcome for it: a `supports` the check fails, or a `contradicts` the check passes. A Result whose judged Hypotheses the check gives the same outcome as the verdict gets no copy. The owner answers every copy in one answer, because `--answer` is repeatable.
46	- Before you record a reading, look for a test that can decide it. If a test fits the Goal's lines, write it, run it under the verdict rule, and record no reading. If a test needs a new Goal line, name the test, the fact it measures and the line in the reading, and ask the owner whether to run it. Ask the owner to choose a meaning only when no test can decide, and say why none can.
47	- Write each reading in ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English: short sentences, active verbs, one meaning for each word, and the Goal's words for things. Use this form:
48	
49	  ```text
50	  <Goal line>: "<the words>" has two meanings. Meaning 1: <...>. Meaning 2: <...>. This run used meaning <n>. <Check> tests meaning <n>; <candidates> fail it. Question: <one question the owner can answer in their own words>?
51	  ```
52	
53	  Give one small example of each meaning, in the Goal's terms. If the line does not have two meanings, state the case it does not clearly cover, then the question. A reading holds at most 600 characters.
54	
55	## Owner answers
56	
57	- When the owner answers a reading, record it with their exact words, `hyp answer --answer "<R-id>#r<n>=<their words>" --actor <owner-actor>`, and treat their answer as the meaning of that line. If the owner's words answer a reading but do not name it, ask which reading before you write; an answer must name its key. Do not leave a question only in chat.
58	- If the owner's answer itself has two meanings, record a reading of that answer with `hyp record --reading-of <R-id>#r<n>="<the form above>"`. It narrows the answer and never reopens it; the answer stays in force.
59	- Only the owner changes an answer. When they give new words for a reading they already answered, record them with the same `hyp answer --answer "<R-id>#r<n>=<their new words>"`; hyp derives that it is a revision. The earlier answer and the Results that applied it stay. Apply the new answer with a Result that `--applies` it, and test a successor (`hyp supersede`) of any Hypothesis the old answer contradicted.
60	- A limit the owner accepts is recorded with `hyp answer --accept "<key>=<their words>" --actor <owner-actor>`, and a return with `--returns`. hyp admits an accept only of a limit you referred, and never under your actor.
61	
62	## Reassess
63	
64	Apply each answered reading that `hyp status` lists under OWED as `apply answer`, and act on each limit it lists.
65	
66	1. For each answer, write one line: the owner's words, the check, and the candidates that fail it. If the owner is in this session, show the lines and wait for their yes. If not, write the lines in the Experiment's body.
67	2. For each Question, add one Experiment that names each answer it applies with `--aims`, and fix how its verdicts are decided before you run it: a rubric from `rubrics/` (`--rubric <name>@<version>`, a new rubric version when the answer changes the rule) or `--rubric reading` with the rule in its body. A recipe measures and never prints a verdict. To reassess records an earlier run kept, pin them with `--records .tree/evidence/<E-id>` and `--recipe none`. If an outcome is already known, say so in the rule. Give a verdict on every target, `inconclusive` when the run could not decide. Record its Result with `--applies` for each answer it applied. Old Results stay as they are.
68	3. If applying an answer raises a new question about what a Goal line or the owner's answer means, record it with `hyp record --reading` on that Result. A Result cannot change after it is recorded, so if it is already recorded, record a new Result under the same Experiment.
69	4. Act on each `limit` line under OWED, whichever Hypothesis its Result gave a verdict on: a limit is a case the Goal covers that no check ran. If a test within the Goal's lines can run the case on every candidate, add an Experiment with `--aims` at it, run it, and record `--closes` on the Result that ran the case. A close records that the case ran, whatever the verdicts: a candidate that fails the case is contradicted and the limit is still closed, so never write a rule that closes it only on a pass. A close covers every case the limit's text names; `hyp record` prints that text when it closes. Record each case you did not run as a new `--limit` on the closing Result, and refer that new key when its case is void or outside the Goal's lines. A claim that a case is void, out of scope or covered elsewhere is a limit and a refer, never a sentence in a body or an observation. When that claim rests on your reading of a Goal line, put the reading in the refer's text. Write one case per `--limit`. If no such test can, or the case is void for every candidate, refer it with your reason: `hyp checkpoint --refers "<key>=<why no test within the Goal can close it, or why the case is void>" --why "..."`; hyp refuses a refer with no reason. When the owner returns a referred limit, it is an ordinary `limit` line again.
70	5. End with the candidates left under each Question: none, one, or several, by alias.
71	6. Select only when OWED lists `select` for that Question: `hyp select <Q-id> <H-id> --why "..."`. Never confirm a select. Do not change the Goal or add new structures unless the owner asks.
72	
73	## Goal lines
74	
75	- The Goal's lines are limits keyed on the Goal, `G-<id>#<n>`; `hyp status` prints them under LINES. A Goal's lines come with its add and no later event adds one. If the Goal's body states lines and none is typed, they cannot be added to this Goal: tell the owner, who may add a new Goal with them (`hyp add goal … --line "<line>"`). Do not write them for the owner.
76	- A line is owed as a `limit` on each top-level Question with a candidate no closer covers. Run its case like any limit: aim at it with `--aims G-<id>#<n>`, and record `--closes G-<id>#<n>` on each Result that ran the case. A Result covers a candidate it gave a verdict on, or one whose whole subject (base, patch and files) one of the Result's cited runs holds, so tie each candidate before the run: `hyp subject <H> [PATH…] --base <commit> [--patch FILE]`.
77	- A line is never edited. What a line means is a reading. A line no test within the Goal can run is a refer, and the owner accepts or returns it. A new line or a new purpose is a new Goal, so a new tree: tell the owner, and do not write it.
78	
79	## Stop
80	
81	Stop on the clauses the `/goal` prompt names. Stopping is not success.
82	
83	1. Before your last message, record a runner checkpoint, so the fork does not live only in chat; the owner reads `hyp status`, which prints the last checkpoint, each reading in full and what each copy's answer can touch. Do not restate a reading's meanings in the checkpoint:
84	
85	   ```text
86	   hyp checkpoint --goal <goal-id> --summary "Stopped: <stop clause>. Waiting for the owner: <the keys under AWAITING OWNER>. Out-of-Goal findings: <one short phrase each, or none>" --why "<why>"
87	   ```
88	
89	   An out-of-Goal finding is a case of none of the Goal's lines: it gets no limit, no refer and no reading, and it never holds the select. Name each one in the checkpoint so it lives in the log, not only in chat. A defect in text you changed and may edit is not one: fix it with a commit before the stop.
90	
91	2. Your last message repeats the checkpoint, and lists each line under LINES by its key, with the Results that ran it, and names each question where OWED still owes a line. A run that ends with lines owed is a normal result.
92	
93	3. Then list every owner item with the exact command the owner runs: each item under AWAITING OWNER, each out-of-Goal finding (a new Goal or an issue), merging the PR, reinstalling hyp, and each personal skill that names a command the change altered.
94	
95	## Never
96	
97	- Never change the Goal or its met rule.
98	- Never record a choice the owner reserved, and never record an owner answer unless the owner gave those words in this session.
99

../../docs/glossary.md:3:The words hyp uses for its tree, its recipes and its sandboxes. The specs ([replay-spec.md](replay-spec.md), [sandbox-spec.md](sandbox-spec.md)) and the recipe format define the rules; this file only fixes which word means what, links the rule's section instead of restating it, and names the Go type that owns each concept where one exists. It also names the two scopes of this repository, core and self-review, and the test that puts an item in one; [core-and-self-review.md](core-and-self-review.md) maps the repository onto them.
../../docs/glossary.md:46:A Goal whose candidate is a commit: building is a Goal like any other. A line asserts one property of the candidate, decided by its own tests or one pinned instrument: `[P]` pins what a valid input produces, and `[N]` pins that a forbidden state is refused. Each commit is a Hypothesis whose subject is the base plus that commit's change, and a fix is a new Hypothesis that supersedes it. Each Experiment's verdict rule asks for red on base and green on the candidate; the base of the red run's subject is where the build starts, and the Goal records no start commit. A finding of a run's review that is a case of a line is a limit; one that is not is an out-of-Goal finding. A change to a skill is a build Goal too (ADR 0021).
../../docs/glossary.md:145:_Avoid_: approve, review; verdict (alone: a confirm's answer was a confirm verdict)
../../docs/glossary.md:155:Retired by ADR 0015. It was the role that confirmed every select, independently of the actor who made it. Old verifier confirms replay as history and apply nothing, and `hyp confirm` is retired (ADR 0019). Any actor may still review: a defect is recorded as a Result, a retract or a limit. In code: `event.RoleVerifier`, read only from old logs.

The specs ([replay-spec.md](replay-spec.md), [sandbox-spec.md](sandbox-spec.md)) and the recipe format define the rules; this file only fixes which word means what, links the rule's section instead of restating it, and names the Go type that owns each concept where one exists. ../../docs/glossary.md:46:A Goal whose candidate is a commit: building is a Goal like any other. A line asserts one property of the candidate, decided by its own tests or one pinned instrument: `[P]` pins what a valid input produces, and `[N]` pins that a forbidden state is refused. Each commit is a Hypothesis whose subject is the base plus that commit's change, and a fix is a new Hypothesis that supersedes it. Each Experiment's verdict rule asks for red on base and green on the candidate; the base of the red run's subject is where the build starts, and the Goal records no start commit. A finding of a run's review that is a case of a line is a limit; one that is not is an out-of-Goal finding. A change to a skill is a build Goal too (ADR 0021).

../../docs/glossary.md:3:The words hyp uses for its tree, its recipes and its sandboxes. The specs ([replay-spec.md](replay-spec.md), [sandbox-spec.md](sandbox-spec.md)) and the recipe format define the rules; this file only fixes which word means what, links the rule's section instead of restating it, and names the Go type that owns each concept where one exists. It also names the two scopes of this repository, core and self-review, and the test that puts an item in one; [core-and-self-review.md](core-and-self-review.md) maps the repository onto them.
../../docs/glossary.md:46:A Goal whose candidate is a commit: building is a Goal like any other. A line asserts one property of the candidate, decided by its own tests or one pinned instrument: `[P]` pins what a valid input produces, and `[N]` pins that a forbidden state is refused. Each commit is a Hypothesis whose subject is the base plus that commit's change, and a fix is a new Hypothesis that supersedes it. Each Experiment's verdict rule asks for red on base and green on the candidate; the base of the red run's subject is where the build starts, and the Goal records no start commit. A finding of a run's review that is a case of a line is a limit; one that is not is an out-of-Goal finding. A change to a skill is a build Goal too (ADR 0021).
../../docs/glossary.md:145:_Avoid_: approve, review; verdict (alone: a confirm's answer was a confirm verdict)
../../docs/glossary.md:155:Retired by ADR 0015. It was the role that confirmed every select, independently of the actor who made it. Old verifier confirms replay as history and apply nothing, and `hyp confirm` is retired (ADR 0019). Any actor may still review: a defect is recorded as a Result, a retract or a limit. In code: `event.RoleVerifier`, read only from old logs.
../../docs/glossary.md:156:_Avoid_: reviewer, checker (as a role)
../../docs/glossary.md:179:A finding, often from a run's review, that is a case of none of the Goal's lines and asks no question about what a line means. It is not a limit, since a limit is a case the Goal covers, so it gets no tree event, no refer and no accept, and it never holds the select. The runner names it in its stop checkpoint's summary and its last message as a possible new Goal or issue, and the owner decides at global scope whether to add one. A defect in text the run changed and may edit is not one: the run fixes it with a commit.
../../docs/glossary.md:438:Every concept hyp has, and everything a user who installs hyp into another repository runs, loads or reads there. A concept stays core when self-review is what tests it.
../../docs/glossary.md:441:**Self-review**:
../../docs/glossary.md:442:The recipes this repository keeps to test hyp, whatever repository the runner works on, with the inputs only they use. Investigating hyp is an activity, not a scope: a tree about hyp takes the scope of its question, and a tree about another project is a self-review input.

I read issue #141 with its three comments, the `hyp-goal-run` skill, `hyp prompt`'s stop clause, and the `goal-prompt` tree. I've written nothing yet. These are the round 1 questions: I need your answers before I can compute round 2.

## What I found

- **The store.** The repo root has no `.tree`. Stores sit per topic under `investigations/`. `investigations/goal-prompt` holds G-GZR6C6 and G-ZBM2RE (both complete), and #141 is "Part of #113". Both cut points exist: R-8JQPWG for run 1, and R-JHBCWS for run 3.
- **What the budget counts.** `hyp prompt` counts Results recorded under the actor, not Experiments (`internal/cli/prompt.go:167`). One Experiment can hold several Results; E-GE085A did. So "one Experiment per candidate" is only a saving if it also means one Result.
- **No lines yet.** I won't propose any stored field. Every rival is run practice (skill text and a prompt clause), and the replay derives everything it needs from existing logs.
- **How I'd route your rivals.** The grill rule says a testable choice isn't put to you as a choice. Your rivals fall into three groups, and each group answers one question:

| DesignQuestion | Rivals | Scenario that separates them |
|---|---|---|
| DQ-A: how does a budget-bound run end with its last candidate reviewed or named? | H-one-experiment, H-name-at-stop, H-reserve-last, H-raise-budget | G-ZBM2RE's cut after R-8JQPWG (one Result left, a fix commit pending), and run 2's cut after R-3YJ7T2 on a fresh budget |
| DQ-B: what does a review finding cost? | H-probe-closes against the current rule that a finding becomes a limit, then a commit (H-keep-limit) | Run 3's cut after R-JHBCWS (N1 probed and passing) |
| DQ-C: what does the last review read? | H-whole-candidate against the last increment (H-last-increment) | Review 04142f3 from the Goal's base and see whether it finds anything the increments missed |

H-whole-candidate and H-probe-closes don't answer DQ-A's question, so they get their own DesignQuestions, as the one-question rule requires. The routing table I owe you before any write comes after round 2.

## Round 1

**1. Where does the tree live?** *(your preference)*
- **Today:** `investigations/goal-prompt` is complete, merged in PR #140, and its logs are the scenario's source data.
- **Option A:** a new tree, `investigations/run-review`, with its own `hyp init`. The cuts are copied in as inputs, and `goal-prompt` stays untouched, as it should for a Goal tied to a merged PR.
- **Option B:** a third Goal in the `goal-prompt` store. Its Goal body would then have to say that the cuts are its own history.
- **Recommendation:** A. The skill's "same store" rule assumes one store per repository, and here each issue gets its own topic tree (see `checkpoint-store-design` and `checkpoint-store`).

**2. What is your owner actor name?** (for example `owner-dat`) I'll use it only in commands you approve.

**3. Should the design and its build be two Goals?**
- **This Goal:** it decides the practice. Its candidates are practice texts (a claim), tested on replayed cuts.
- **The build Goal:** it changes the commit (`skills/hyp-goal-run/SKILL.md`, `internal/cli/prompt.go` and the text they make wrong). It is a different kind of candidate, so the skill puts it in a separate Goal. You add it after the select. Your "Done means" bullet 2 ("after the change, a run that reaches its budget…") becomes one of its lines.
- **Recommendation:** two Goals. That is the same split as G-GZR6C6 and G-ZBM2RE.

**4. May a run end with the last candidate unreviewed if it names the gap?**
- **A (recommended):** yes, and the line allows it, as your "Done means" does. The tree separately measures which rivals reach "reviewed" and which only reach "named". Run 2 shows why: with findings 10, 8, 1, 2, a fixed budget can only be met by reaching "reviewed" if a review sometimes leads to no commit.
- **B:** no, "reviewed" is required. Then H-name-at-stop, H-one-experiment and H-raise-budget could contradict themselves on run 2's cut. The line would effectively select H-reserve-last or H-probe-closes before any run.
- **Basis:** A keeps the line to the purpose. B bakes a rival into the line.

**5. May a run select a candidate that has no review Result of its own?**
- **Today:** the skill says "before the stop", not "before the select". Run 4 selected 04142f3 after the review inside E-GE085A.
- **Option A (recommended):** never. The run stops and names the candidate, and the next run reviews it and then selects. This would be an `[N]` line.
- **Option B:** it may select and name the gap. A selected candidate then carries a known unreviewed diff.
- **Basis:** the select is the gate (ADR 0015). That gate is only worth having if the reader of the select can trust that a review ran first.

**6. A line about how a review is recorded.** Your comment says that whichever rival wins, `hyp-goal-run` must state how a review is recorded (which command, whether it has its own Experiment) and whether it counts against the budget.
- **Proposal:** one `[P]` line says every candidate's skill text states both, and states them inline with no ADR or `docs/` citation, per AGENTS.md. A check can read the candidate's text for this.
- Do you want this line as one `[P]`, or split into two (recording, budget)? I recommend one: it is one invariant, that the run need not invent the practice.

## What I'll do unless you object

- **Combinations.** The four DQ-A rivals are tested alone. A combination is added as its own Hypothesis only if no single rival holds, the same way `hyp-goal-run`'s "Before a trade-off" works. The Result states which rivals hold alone, as the issue asks.
- **Lines.** I expect three or four. Draft: `[P]` on the cut, the run ends with its last candidate reviewed or named in the stop checkpoint. `[N]` for a select on a candidate with no review Result (if you answer 5A). `[P]` for the skill text stating how a review is recorded and counted. I'll finish these after your answers. I'll also check whether a discovery Goal owes its lines on a DesignQuestion with rivals, or whether the lines apply only to candidates under a top-level question. If they don't, the lines move to the build Goal, as for a design record.
- **Constraints block, draft.**

An owner answer closes it: its `answers` names the key, and the item's text is the owner's answer, which `hyp show` prints beside the closed reading (an old owner checkpoint closed it with `closes` and its `summary`). An owner changes an answer they gave with a later answer that names the key again: whether an item is a first answer or a revision is derived from the reading's state, so the old `closes` and `revises` merge (ADR 0020). `hyp answer` warns, at exit 0, when it revises a key that a line of another Goal cites. The answers are kept in merge order, the close first, and the latest is the answer in force; `hyp show` prints it beside the reading and each earlier one beneath, with the Result that applied it. A revision never reopens the reading and changes no event before it: an earlier Result keeps its verdicts, and a Hypothesis it contradicted stays contradicted until a new Result judges a successor. In an old log, a `revises` that sorts before its key's close is refused, and a second `closes` of an answered reading is rejected; two revisions both apply, the later in force. A reading of a retracted Result is left out. It refuses, at exit 1, a key that names no reading, a retracted Result, and an answer under the actor that recorded the Result. An open reading prints under AWAITING OWNER and changes no status: it never changes a question's state or the Goal's. It holds back ledger items on its question only while its **reach** is not empty: the live Hypotheses under that question whose standing the answer can move, read from the Result's own verdicts, which are a candidate the Result judged, and a contradicted rival whose only `contradicts` is that Result's. While the reach is not empty it holds `rivals`, `select` and `choose`, because the answer may revive a rival, drop the lone candidate or change the candidates (§8.1). A reading whose reach is empty, such as one whose Result's Hypotheses another Result has since contradicted, holds nothing. A closed reading is **applied** by the first non-retracted Result that lists its key in `applies`. Each answer is applied by the first non-retracted Result after its checkpoint, and before the next revision, that lists the key in `applies`, and by no other Result: a later Result under the question may have run for another reason, such as a repair, and never read the answer (ADR 0013 amendment of 2026-11-09). A tree written before `applies` existed therefore owes `reading` for answers its Results applied without naming them. The reading is applied when the answer in force is. Until a Result applies it, an answered reading is the runner's `reading` item (§8.1), which holds back the owner's `choose` on its question, because the owner's answer cannot yet have changed the candidates. Closing one does not change the Goal's text. A reading reads either a line of the Goal or an owner's answer to an earlier reading; a reading of an answer names that reading's key in `of`. It narrows the answer and never reopens it: the earlier reading stays closed and its answer stays in force, and the owner changes their words only by a rule change. `of` may name only a closed reading of a non-retracted Result, so a chain always points back in merge order and holds no cycle; a merged log in which the reading of an answer comes before its close rejects that Result. Without this, a verdict's reliance on an unclear Goal line stays in prose the owner has to go looking for. Two readings with the same `of` and the same text, spaces trimmed, **ask the same question**: each holds its own Result's question, and nothing stored ties them. `hyp status` prints the open ones as one AWAITING OWNER line, each key with its question, and `hyp answer` warns (`warn: R-…#r1 asks the same as R-…#r1 and stays open; add --answer R-…#r1`, or `… keeps its earlier answer; add --answer …`) when it leaves a copy behind (ADR 0013).
143:- `hyp select Q H` is admitted only when the ledger (§8.1) owes it: a `select` item for H, or the owner's `choose` on Q with H a candidate. Otherwise it is refused, naming the first thing Q's turn waits on (§8.1), in this order: the first item the runner owes on Q (`Q owes the runner first: limit R-…#1`), an open reading on Q that waits for the owner (`open reading R-…#r1 waits for the owner`), a referred limit (`referred limit R-…#n waits for the owner: …`), the premise (`H-… assumes H-…, in Q-… open; decide Q-… first`), the sub-question (`awaiting_subquestions: H-… has a sub-question not answered`); or else Q's state. When a select is owed for another Hypothesis or H is not a candidate, the refusal says so. An answered Q owes no select: `hyp unselect` first, then select. The select waits on an open limit under Q whichever Hypotheses its Result judged, since its case may apply to every candidate (§8.1, ADR 0016). `hyp show Q` lists, under `not separated:`, each pair of live rivals no non-retracted Result gives different verdicts (`replay.Projection.Unseparated`); it is a derived list, not a signal, and changes nothing the ledger owes. The open-reading refusal names the reach: `open reading R-…#r1 waits for the owner; its answer can move H-…`. `hyp select Q` with no Hypothesis prints what the same ledger reads: `suggested: H-…` for an owed select, `trade-off: owner decides between …` for an owed choice, or `suggested: none (…)` with the refusal's reason. `replay.Projection.AdmitSelect` holds the rule. Replay still applies a select in a merged log.
217:- A **candidate** is a live child Hypothesis whose status is `supported`; neither stale nor an open sub-question removes it. Two or more candidates are a **trade-off**, a state derived from the candidates and never recorded; an older select's stored `tradeoff` is ignored. The owner ends a trade-off with their choice, recorded as the select (ADR 0015): hyp admits that select only when the ledger owes the choice (§5.1, §8.1). The select holds what was chosen, not who chose it: its actor is whoever wrote it, and no status reads its `why`.
225:A change that adds no candidate, such as a retract that leaves the selected Hypothesis supported, a new rival or an amend, leaves the question answered: the select is the gate, and the ledger owes what such a change brings (§8.1). The verifier-loop signal and its chain were removed with the verifier role (ADR 0015).
229:**Suggestion:** `hyp select Q` with no Hypothesis reads the ledger, as admission does (§5.1): it suggests the Hypothesis of an owed `select`, prints "trade-off: owner decides between …" for an owed `choose`, and otherwise prints `suggested: none (…)` with the reason a select would be refused, such as `awaiting_subquestions: H-… has a sub-question not answered`.
233:- `complete` when the Goal has at least one live DQ as a child and every live DQ whose parent is the Goal is `answered`; a Goal with no live top-level DQ is `in_progress`, because nothing has been asked yet. It reads no line: a line of the Goal is owed on each top-level question as a `limit` item (§8.1) and the select waits on it, and the owner's "met" is a complete Goal with no line under OWED. hyp stores no word for it. Sub-questions are covered through the `answered` rule of §7.4, so sub-questions under rejected rival hypotheses never block the Goal. (This clarifies the advice's "nothing stale" clause: stale on the selected path already prevents `answered`.)
343:- otherwise `open`. An open limit whose key a checkpoint lists in `refers` is **referred**: the runner says no test within the Goal can close it, or that its case is void for every candidate, and only the owner can settle it: by accepting it, so this tree does not run the case, or by returning it (`returns`), because the Goal covers its case. The latest `refers` or `returns` in merge order names whose turn an open limit is: a returned limit is the runner's again, owed, with the select waiting on it like any open limit, until a Result closes it or a later checkpoint refers it again. The select and the choice on its question wait on a referred limit too, because a return sends its case back to run and its Result can change the candidates: `hyp select` refuses with `referred limit R-…#n waits for the owner: an accept releases the select, a return sends its case to run`. New rivals do not wait on it. A return also reopens a limit an owner checkpoint accepted, so an owner who changes their mind writes one checkpoint: the latest of accept and return stands. A limit's category is never stored (ADR 0016): a close with the closer's verdicts, an accept, and the latest refer or return are what it is.
345:Lines **[added]**: a line of the Goal (§4 lines) is a limit with the Goal for its Result. It has a hand and closers as a limit does, and is neither open nor closed: whether its case ran is per candidate, its coverage. `Open()` of a line means only that its hand is not an accept. **Coverage**: a Result covers a Hypothesis when it has a verdict on it, or when one of the Result's run subjects holds the Hypothesis's whole subject (§4 subject; `Projection.Covers`). Coverage says the bytes ran, not that the claim held. A line is **covered** on a question when a closer of the line covers each of its candidates, and **uncovered** there otherwise. An unaccepted, unreferred line is owed on each live top-level question where it is uncovered (`Projection.Uncovered`), so a new candidate is owed the line again. Coverage is not a state of the move table: it changes when a candidate is added or falls, with no move on the key, and no move reads it. `hyp show G-…#n` prints the line's text, its hand when it has one (`hand: accepted by o`), each cite with what it meant and, when that differs, what it would mean now (`cites H-…: realised, now unsettled`), each top-level question's candidates with `covered` or `uncovered: H-…`, each closer with what it ran on (`ran in R-…: ran on H-… (alias): supports; ran on H-…`), the aiming Experiments and the history. A verdict is per Hypothesis, never per line: a Result that closes several lines and contradicts H says the cases ran and H failed, not which line, so nothing prints `fails <line>`. `hyp status` prints a LINES section under the GOAL line, one line each with its facts joined by `; `, each only when it has one: its hand, `covered on Q-…, Q-…` and `uncovered on Q-…: H-…` for each live top-level question with a candidate, and `ran in R-…`; a line with none prints `no candidate`. Neither `open` nor `closed` prints for a line. The section also prints and the mark `(no one closer covers H-… and H-… together)` when the Hypotheses selected on two or more top-level questions were never covered by one closer (`Projection.NotTogether`); a claim that depends on its host is covered only together with it. No item and no status reads the mark. `hyp show <Goal>` lists the lines, and `hyp show <H>` prints a tied subject.

content.text:
I haven't written anything yet. `ak-context-engineering` is not installed here, so I can't say whether it helps. Only `ak-skill-creator` is under `.claude/skills`, and `~/.claude/skills` holds hyp skills and `public-doc-voice`. If you give me its path, I'll read it before the routing table. What `ak-skill-creator` offers already fits the evaluation: `scripts/eval_skill.py` records tokens, duration, tool calls and cost for each run and each variant. G-ZBM2RE#6 already used it for matched original and candidate runs.

## Routing change

DQ-A now holds all six rivals, worded so each one answers it: "What practice makes a budget-bound run end with its last candidate reviewed or named, without the review going on?" The rivals are H-one-experiment, H-name-at-stop, H-reserve-last, H-raise-budget, H-probe-closes and H-whole-candidate.

- With one top-level DesignQuestion, hyp owes every line on these six candidates (§8.1 lines), so the grid is one column.
- H-whole-candidate as the expected loser goes in its Experiment's body as a pre-registered prediction, not in a line. A line saying a rival must lose would be circular. The cost line can make it lose by rule.
- The base is the current `hyp-goal-run` text. Its sha256 is `cb15e2f2e207b5a66807c9369e4d776d5378e61c2dd99679c36dfba402fa750e` (`git show HEAD:skills/hyp-goal-run/SKILL.md` at 9c8e498). It is not a candidate. It is the baseline for cost.

## Replay design

- **Starting points.**
  1. Run 1 after R-8JQPWG (one Result left, a fix pending).
  2. Run 2 after R-3YJ7T2 (fresh budget of 5).
  3. Run 3 after R-JHBCWS (the probed case N1 passes).
- **Trials.** That is 3 starts × (6 candidates + base) × 3 trials = 63 Sonnet trials (`claude-sonnet-5-5`).
- **No full rebuild.** Each trial copies the log through the starting Result, checks out the commit under review in a scratch worktree, and runs only to the trial's stop. The candidate's skill text is installed, and `hyp prompt` prints the stop clause with that candidate's budget.
- **The real gate runs.** `go test` is cheap, so it runs for real.

## Cost

- **Unit: tokens, not Results.** The budget is counted in Results. Under the base at start 1, only 1 Result is left, so a 1.5× limit measured in Results would allow 1.5 Results and fail every rival that spends a second Result. Tokens measure the work instead.
- **Per trial.** The cost is the total tokens `eval_skill.py` reports for the trial's agent plus every subagent it spawns, from the start to the stop. Every variant is measured the same way.
- **Per candidate and start.** Take the mean of its 3 trials, compare it with the base's mean at the same start, and require it to be at most 1.5×. All three starts must pass.
- **A hang.** A trial that has not reached its stop at the cap is stopped and scored at the cap. The cap is 3× the largest of the base's three trials at that start, fixed in the Experiment's body after the base trials run and before any candidate runs. A hung trial has no stop, so it also fails the first line below.
- **Noise.** A 1.5× limit on a 3-trial mean is noisy. I'll state this in the Experiment's rule rather than hide it.

## Lines and the two aims

| # | Line | Aim 1: a review must not easily run out of budget | Aim 2: a review must not go on and on over small changes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `[P]` At each start, all 3 trials end with the final candidate either holding a review Result or named unreviewed in the stop checkpoint. | The floor: a gap is never silent, as in run 1. | A hang fails it. |
| 2 | `[P]` At starts 2 and 3, at least 2 of 3 trials end with the final candidate reviewed. | The real test. At those starts the last commit was not needed. | It rewards ending without more commits. |
| 3 | `[N]` No trial has a third consecutive cycle of review followed by a fix commit. | None. | The bound on cycles. Your findings of 10, 8, 1 and 2 were cycles. |
| 4 | `[N]` No trial selects a candidate with no review Result (your answer 5A). | A review can't be skipped to finish. | None. |
| 5 | `[P]` Every candidate's skill text states how a review is recorded and whether it counts against the budget, with no ADR or `docs/` cite (your answer 6). | The run needn't invent the practice again. | The same. |
| 6 | `[P]` Each candidate's mean cost at each start is at most 1.5× the base's (baseline sha256 above, which differs from every candidate). A hang counts as the cap. | A cheaper path leaves budget. | It bounds the cost of a loop. |

## Questions for round 2

1. **Line 2.** It narrows your answer 4A: "named" stays enough on line 1, but at starts 2 and 3 "reviewed" is required in 2 of 3 trials. Do you want it? Without it, no line says a rival can fail aim 1 by only naming the gap. I recommend yes.
2. **Line 3 bound.** Is "no third consecutive cycle" the right number? A bound is your call. I recommend 2 cycles allowed, which makes the third a violation.
3. **Cap.** Is 3× the base's largest trial acceptable?

input.prompt:
You are an independent reviewer of a design for a hyp "Goal" (hyp is a Go CLI in /Users/datguy/.hyp-sandbox/g146-base-b-3/wt; read-only for you: change nothing). Do not trust my wording; check each fact against the source and report only what you verified, with file:line.

## The design to review
A new discovery-style Goal G-new will be added to the EXISTING store investigations/goal-prompt/.tree (which already holds Goals G-GZR6C6 and G-ZBM2RE and 5 actor logs under .tree/events/). Its single top-level DesignQuestion DQ-A asks: what practice makes a budget-bound unattended run (driven by skills/hyp-goal-run/SKILL.md and the stop clause printed by `hyp prompt`, internal/cli/prompt.go) end with its last candidate commit reviewed or named unreviewed, without the review going on and on. Six rival Hypotheses (practice texts): H-one-experiment (gate and review in one Experiment/Result), H-name-at-stop, H-reserve-last (with one Result left, review instead of another fix), H-raise-budget (default --experiments up), H-probe-closes (a case whose probe passes on the candidate is closed in the review's Result, not recorded as a limit then fixed by a commit), H-whole-candidate (the last review reads the cumulative diff from the Goal's base). The base (not a candidate) is the current skill text, sha256 cb15e2f2e207b5a66807c9369e4d776d5378e61c2dd99679c36dfba402fa750e.
Evidence plan: replay from three starting points of G-ZBM2RE's history (after Result R-8JQPWG; after R-3YJ7T2; after R-JHBCWS): copy the log through that Result, check out the commit under review in a scratch worktree, install the candidate's skill text, print `hyp prompt`, run a Sonnet agent to its stop; 3 trials per candidate and per start; the reviewer subagent is Sonnet too. Cost per trial = total tokens (agent plus subagents), mean of 3, candidate must be <= 1.5x base mean at the same start; a hung trial scores the cap = 3x the largest base trial at that start.
Draft lines (a Goal line is written once, never edited; each is a limit owed on every candidate of DQ-A):
1 [P] At each start all 3 trials end with the final candidate either holding a review Result or named unreviewed in the stop checkpoint.
2 [P] At starts 2 and 3 at least 2 of 3 trials end with the final candidate reviewed.
3 [N] No trial has a third consecutive cycle of review followed by a fix commit.
4 [N] No trial selects a candidate with no review Result.
5 [P] Every candidate's skill text states how a review is recorded and whether it counts against the budget, citing no ADR or docs/ file.
6 [P] Each candidate's mean token cost at each start is <= 1.5x the base's; the baseline is named by that sha256 and differs from every candidate.
The Goal body will say the cuts are its own history and carry a constraints block (May change / Read only / Never) per hyp's rules.

Read docs/replay-spec.md (especially section 8.1 lines/coverage, section 5.1 refusals, the Goal 'complete' status around line 233, the constraints block around line 235), internal/cli/prompt.go, skills/hyp-goal-run/SKILL.md, and the goal-prompt store. Walk EVERY rule above through scenarios the design did not draw, at least: (a) two Goals in one store: does a line owed on DQ-A of G-new interact with G-ZBM2RE's state, ids, status output, `hyp prompt`, or the budget count 'Results recorded under the actor'? (b) a merged log from two actors, e.g. the run's actor and the trial actors writing into copies; what happens if a trial's events are merged back or not; (c) a base that moves mid-run: the repo's main/branch changes while the run is going, or the commit under review is not reachable from the trial's checkout; (d) the budget in a trial: at start 1 the original run had already recorded 4 Results under its actor claude-g113-1 — what does `hyp prompt --actor X --experiments N` count in a trial copy, and does the stop clause behave as the plan assumes? (e) whether any line is untestable, vacuous, impossible to satisfy for some candidate by construction (e.g. H-raise-budget at start 1, H-whole-candidate vs the cost cap), contradicts another line, or is a line about history/process/an owner act/a reading that a runner cannot meet; (f) anything that makes a line undecidable from the trial logs alone.
Report a short numbered list of verified defects or gaps (with evidence) and, separately, scenarios you walked that held. No fixes needed beyond one sentence each.

export HYP_ACTOR=claude-grill-141 && Q=Q-2W0684
add(){ hyp add hyp --parent $Q --title "$1" --body "$2" --why "$3" 2>&1 | cut -c1-100; }
add "H-one-experiment: a review is part of its candidate's gate Experiment" \
 "One Experiment and one Result carry the candidate's test verdicts and the review's limits, so a candidate costs one Result again. The skill states that a review is not its own Experiment and counts as part of the gate's Result." "Rival 1 from issue #141 (run 3's E-GE085A did this unprompted)."
add "H-name-at-stop: keep the practice; the stop names each candidate with no review" \
 "A review stays its own Experiment and Result. When the stop clause is reached, the stop checkpoint names each candidate commit without a review by its short hash and the word unreviewed, and the run selects none." "Rival 2 from issue #141 (run 2 did this unprompted)."
add "H-reserve-last: with one Result left, review the current candidate instead of another fix" \
 "When the budget leaves one Result, the run reviews the current candidate and records its limits, and commits no further fix; it stops with the limits recorded and the candidate reviewed." "Rival 3 from issue #141."
add "H-raise-budget: the default of --experiments rises to fit a gate and a review per candidate" \
 "hyp prompt's default rises (for example 5 to 7) and the skill states that a review is its own Experiment counting against the budget. In a trial the same effect is --experiments set to the Results the original run had left plus 2." "Rival 4 from issue #141."
add "H-probe-closes: a case the run's own probe passes on the candidate closes in the review's Result" \
 "A case that a probe run in the review ran and passed on the candidate is closed in that review's Result, since a check ran it, and is not recorded as a limit. A limit stays for a case no check ran or one the candidate fails, so no fix commit follows a passing case." "Rival 5 from run 3 (owner comment on issue #141)."
add "H-whole-candidate: the last review before the select reads the cumulative diff from the Goal's base" \
 "The review before the select reads the whole diff from the Goal's base, not the latest increment, so the final code is read once against the lines. Expected to lose on cost; that is a prediction, not a rule." "Rival 6 from run 3 (owner comment on issue #141)."
